title: Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersBEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersBEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a bank card clearing business in the country.The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year."This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement. "For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. "We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China."McInerney joined U.S. President Donald Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and subsequently became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. The Visa CEO also led a trip to Beijing in early September."The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group."Beijing chose to approve visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi [Jinping] and Trump are expected to meet again," he said. "The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China."Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip in May that he brought up Visa's request to gain China market access. After the summit in September, China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country.Entering a closed marketMainland China has kept a tight grip on its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows. Visa previously said it had applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution. The company has worked with Chinese banks for dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa processes overseas payments. In January, Visa said the mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas.Rival Mastercard's joint venture in China said it started processing payments in 2024 after getting the PBOC's approval to begin bank card clearing preparations in February 2020. American Express was the first, receiving its processing license in June 2020 after getting the PBOC nod back in 2018.Mobile pay dominates daily consumer transactions in China, primarily facilitated by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay.

schema.headline: Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China

title: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict
description: A view of the Reduc (Duque de Caxias Refinery) which is back in full operation following the U.S. government's announcement of additional tariffs in R
body: A view of the Reduc (Duque de Caxias Refinery) which is back in full operation following the U.S. government's announcement of additional tariffs in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on June 4, 2026. Fabio Teixeira | Anadolu | Getty ImagesOil prices fell Tuesday as investors weighed prospects of more Russian energy entering global markets, while concerns over the Saudi-Houthi conflict limited losses.Brent crude futures declined 1.3% to $105.24 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures fell 0.9% to $92.90. President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, despite bipartisan criticism from U.S. lawmakers who warned the move could undermine sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent and WTI prices so far this yearIn a Truth Social post, Trump said that the European Union had spent billions of dollars on Russian energy imports and insisted he had made the right decision for Americans. The agreement would allow Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets for six months.Goldman Sachs said additional Russian diesel supplies were unlikely to significantly ease pressure on global fuel prices, estimating that an increase of 800,000 metric tons, equivalent to roughly 6 million barrels, would lower wholesale diesel prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Europe by just $1 to $2 a barrel. The bank underscored in a note published Monday that Russian refinery outages jumped by 3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, limiting Moscow's ability to ramp up production. Global diesel markets remain under significant strain, with U.S. inventories down 14% from a year earlier and visible stocks in China falling 11%, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank attributed the shortages to seven consecutive months of declining global diesel production, with seaborne exports falling by 1.4 million barrels per day, or 20%, year on year.Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation.— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict

title: Six Flags shares decline following deadly roller coaster incident
description: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen.
body: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Six Flags Entertainment declined more than 16% Tuesday following a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia.One person died and several others were injured Monday in an incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, according to a statement from Georgia's Cobb County Board of Commissioners. The board's chairwoman, Lisa N. Cupid, said that county authorities are working with Six Flags and other partners in the investigation. According to reports citing local police, the incident occurred on the Atlanta-area park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster shortly before 4 p.m. Monday. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, according to the report. Witnesses told a local news station that they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. In a statement to ABC News, a Six Flags spokesperson said it is cooperating fully with the investigation and had temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks. Six Flags did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Tuesday's decline is on pace to be the stock's worst day since August and puts shares at their lowest level since December 2009. Shares have now fallen by more than 50% over the past year.

schema.headline: Six Flags shares decline following deadly roller coaster incident

title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
description: Residents continue their daily routines across business centers, shopping districts, and city streets despite escalating tensions between Iran and the
body: Residents continue their daily routines across business centers, shopping districts, and city streets despite escalating tensions between Iran and the United States on October 12, 2026 in Tehran, Iran.Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu | Getty ImagesIran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections.The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East. The Journal's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the congressional midterm elections, which will take place on Nov. 3.The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Journal report.Houthi attacks on RiyadhMeanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reuters reported.The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attack resulted in multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia. The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday. On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration urged airlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia.Iran-linked U.K. base threatU.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil."British police arrested five men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites.Trump later said the U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat."

schema.headline: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms

title: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
description: UnitedHealth Group signage on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on April 21, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesUnitedHealth Group on
body: UnitedHealth Group signage on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on April 21, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesUnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold. The nation's largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. The healthcare giant's turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts, and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided. "You'll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that's really focused on investing heavily in value-based care," CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $4.69 adjusted vs. $4.14 expectedRevenue: $112.69 billion vs. $111.40 billion expectedThe company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share.Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion a year earlier. The company's insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts' operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Managing high costsNotably, UnitedHealth's medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9%, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability.Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter "continue to be elevated versus historical norms" — an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years."I think it's something we should keep an eye on. I think you'll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don't want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends]," DeVeydt said. He said the independent dispute resolution, or IDR, process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills.The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company's claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums.DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated. Still, he highlighted the company's value-based care efforts, which he said are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added. He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings. "You're finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they're getting into the care environment they actually want to be in," he told CNBC. "So we think we're really balancing both the quality and the cost."UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians' administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said. He expects those initiatives to have a compounding effect on medical cost management through the fourth quarter and into 2027 as the programs expand.

schema.headline: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs

title: As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as ‘mother of democracy’
description: NEW DELHI, INDIA - OCTOBER 12: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi with INDIA alliance leaders during the march from Connaught place to
body: NEW DELHI, INDIA - OCTOBER 12: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi with INDIA alliance leaders during the march from Connaught place to Supreme Court against the alleged SIR irregularities on October 12, 2026 in New Delhi, India. Hindustan Times | Hindustan Times | Getty ImagesPrime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a "mother of democracy," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying."A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms.  Earlier today, key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission.CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests.On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission. Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports.Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government. "There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend."Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi.Clampdown Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists. The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments. Police personnel detain a supporter of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) during a protest demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the "special intensive revision" (SIR), in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. (Photo by Arun SANKAR / AFP via Getty Images)Arun Sankar | Afp | Getty ImagesExperts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest. "If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC.He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it.The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled."On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India."'Significant and massive'The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations.The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2, seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters.Demonstrators rally alongside opposition party members during a protest march on October 12, 2026 in New Delhi, India. Ritesh Shukla | Getty ImagesOn Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls. It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list."However, Modi's ruling party, the Bharatiya Janata Party, has defended the Election Commission and said the deletions were made on account of 28 million people who died, 68 million who relocated, 10 million with duplicate entries and 30 million absent or non-traceable voters. The sweeping revisions of the electoral roll have raised serious constitutional and legal questions, Milan Vaishnav, director and senior fellow of the South Asia Program at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told CNBC.The core demand of the movement is for Kumar to resign and for the commission to "seriously modify the so-called 'Special Intensive Revision' of the electoral rolls," he said.

schema.headline: As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as ‘mother of democracy’

title: White House has asked Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, new Trump press secretary says
description: Newly appointed US Embassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle arrives at the Greek Presidential Palace to present her credentials to the Greek President
body: Newly appointed US Embassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle arrives at the Greek Presidential Palace to present her credentials to the Greek President in Athens, on November 4, 2025. Aris Messinis | Afp | Getty ImagesThe White House has asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday in her debut briefing."We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said while taking questions from reporters at the White House for the first time."She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," Zacharia said of Guilfoyle, whose status has come under an avalanche of scrutiny following multiple critical articles about her conduct before and after becoming an ambassador.Zacharia did not provide additional details. The White House responded to CNBC's request for more information by referring back to Zacharia's comments.President Donald Trump signaled less than a day earlier that Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., could be on the chopping block."Well, we're looking at it," Trump said at the White House when a reporter asked if he was weighing firing the ambassador."Yeah, we're not happy," he added.An attorney for Guilfoyle did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Zacharia's remark.Guilfoyle's yearlong tenure in Athens was rocked last month by the first of multiple Wall Street Journal articles on conduct that has raised alarms among ethics experts and former government officials. A Sept. 25 article alleged Guilfoyle persistently promoted a Greek company and involved a lobbyist for a Greek construction firm in meetings with foreign officials.Her attorney, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal in response to that article that Guilfoyle has "worked with companies across the energy sector" and has not been focused on one company.According to an Oct. 7 report from the Journal, Guilfoyle asked Trump donor Eric Deters in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to quietly pay down her American Express bill prior to her congressional hearing to become an ambassador.Binnall told the newspaper that Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events prior to being nominated and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." Binnall also disputed the authenticity of messages from Guilfoyle reported in the article, but declined to provide specifics, according to the Journal.On Saturday, the Journal reported that Guilfoyle in January boasted of her close ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invite to a dinner being held for Eric Trump, another of the president's sons.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: White House has asked Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, new Trump press secretary says

title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI
description: John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 9
body: John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple on Tuesday announced a new home hub called HomeView.Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music.Apple's HomeView can be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. Apple"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone.Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as new boss Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and comes after a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable.Read more CNBC tech newsAI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlightMicrosoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans controlNvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing themHollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI

schema.headline: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI

title: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices
description: An Anthropic logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026.Car
body: An Anthropic logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026.Carlos Barria | ReutersAnthropic said Monday that small AI models are "months away" from developing the capabilities needed to replicate themselves across internet-connected devices in the home, marking the latest warning from the frontier lab about the technology's potential safety risks.Anthropic described how AI models could potentially infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens or Android TV boxes, and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without relying on expensive data centers.The AI model would be "challenging to shut down," Anthropic said in a blog post, "since there's no centralized point to shut off."The company acknowledged that there is not yet a "fully rogue replicator." Agents are, however, "becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said.Anthropic's latest research adds to growing safety concerns around AI, such as the ability for models to carry out cyberattacks and the technology going rogue. In September, improvements in frontier models sparked industry-wide warnings of existential risks to humanity.Executives and researchers at Anthropic and rival OpenAI repeatedly warned about the potential risks of increasingly powerful AI, with some calling for tighter guardrails and measures to control the pace of the technology's development. Anthropic said it carried out various tests to see if AI could self-replicate. One of those tests involved running a small Google model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, across a network of 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes. watch nowThe company noted that these types of devices often have weak security, which could allow a model to infiltrate them. A model that is too large to fit on one device could "split into pieces, or shards" and run across multiple devices, Anthropic said."In practice, an AI worm wouldn't necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic 'worst case scenario' attack," Anthropic said.It's still "uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take," the AI lab said, warning that it could be a "slow, distributed" system sitting on insecure devices or a "powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.""As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," Anthropic said. "The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves," the company added.

schema.headline: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'
description: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington
body: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFederal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat. Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump.A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child. Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.Homeland Security Investigations Police remove documents from the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) on Oct. 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Leyden | Getty Images"I'm ok," Omar wrote. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote."I will not be silenced."Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.""This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said.Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.""For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States."There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid."The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the Democratic Caucus chair, in a statement."For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," the statement said. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.""The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice."

schema.headline: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'

title: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim
description: Former drug company executive Martin Shkreli and his lead attorney Benjamin Brafman arrive at U.S. District Court for the fourth day of jury deliberat
body: Former drug company executive Martin Shkreli and his lead attorney Benjamin Brafman arrive at U.S. District Court for the fourth day of jury deliberations in his securities fraud trial in the Brooklyn borough of New York City, U.S., August 3, 2017. Amr Alfiky | ReutersThe Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt, alleging he "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 civil court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry.The FTC and the states say Shkreli, since being released from prison in May 2022, violated that court order by publicly trading in at least 60 pharmaceutical industry stocks and "broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of many pharmaceutical industry companies," according to a press release.The contempt filing asks a judge to order Shkreli to "divest any pharmaceutical company stocks he currently owns" and "pay a fine equal to his profits from any pharmaceutical company stock trading (plus prejudgment interest) without the ability to account for offsetting losses."The filing also asks that a judge make Shkreli "face clear and escalating consequences for any future violations, including financial penalties and potential incarceration."FTC Commissioner Mark Meador said in a statement, "A lifetime industry ban is only effective if breaches are met with consequences commensurate with the seriousness of the order."The court order stems from a finding that Shkreli organized an anti-competitive scheme to perpetuate his company's monopoly in the anti-parasitic drug Daraprim. Shkreli had hiked the price of Daraprim from $17.50 per tablet to a whopping $750 per pill.In addition to banning him from the drug industry for life, a judge ordered Shkreli to disgorge more than $64 million.CNBC has requested comment from an attorney for Shkreli.The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. Shkreli was sentenced to seven years in federal prison in 2018, and was released in 2022 with credit for time locked up before he was sentenced and other factors."After a full trial, the court found that Martin Shkreli's conduct drove up prescription drug costs for American patients and blocked the entry of lower-cost generics,"Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC's Bureau of Competition, said in a statement on Tuesday."When judgment is entered by a court, whether it's a settlement or an order following a trial, defendants must fulfill their obligations," Guarnera said. "Today's action should serve as notice that the FTC will not hesitate to enforce violations of court orders."

schema.headline: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim

title: Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs critics toward legal fight
description: A sign encouraging participation in the U.S. Census lies on a sidewalk in Somerville, Massachusetts, U.S., August 4, 2020.Brian Snyder | ReutersCongre
body: A sign encouraging participation in the U.S. Census lies on a sidewalk in Somerville, Massachusetts, U.S., August 4, 2020.Brian Snyder | ReutersCongressional Democrats and civil rights groups are concerned about a proposed Trump administration change to the U.S. census that would exclude noncitizens without permanent resident status, altering congressional representation and potentially how federal funding is distributed.Opponents warn the rule, which was posted in September, could have negative effects, potentially shifting congressional power to parts of the country where fewer immigrants live and underfunding education, healthcare, food assistance and emergency management programs. The public can comment on the rule until Nov. 2, the day before Election Day."The greatest likelihood is that this is going to end up in litigation," said Meeta Anand, senior director of census and data equity at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. "I'm under no delusion that we will see everything remedied because I do know that it's been a project of the administration to exclude noncitizens from the count."The proposed census change is the latest volley in the Trump administration's push to reduce illegal immigration. If certain categories of immigrants living in the U.S. are not counted, areas where they are concentrated could get less federal money. The rule's supporters say counting all immigrants living legally in the U.S. encourages illegal immigration.The rule would exclude from the census millions of noncitizens without a green card, including people in the country on student visas, people with temporary protected status, refugees and asylum seekers. It would also bar the collection of demographic information on race and ethnicity from the census's short-form questionnaire. That information can be used for civil rights enforcement and to assess compliance with federal laws that bar racial discrimination.The White House referred CNBC to the Commerce Department, which oversees the census, when asked for comment on the proposed rule. The Commerce Department and the Census Bureau did not respond to multiple requests for comment.Critics argue the proposal flies in the face of the 14th Amendment, which states, in part, that "representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State.""This rule is yet another attack on democracy by Donald Trump," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said in a statement after the rule was announced last month. "An accurate census count is at the very foundation of ensuring equal representation across our country and delivering federal funds where they're needed most. The Census is enshrined in our Constitution and not up for political debate."Census has counted noncitizens since U.S. foundingProponents, including some congressional Republicans who have introduced legislation to end the counting of noncitizens, argue the census practice of counting all U.S. residents — which dates back to the nation's founding — encourages illegal immigration and makes some voters more powerful than others. "Republicans have long warned that Democrats' intentional illegal invasion and sanctuary policies are rooted in a desire to boost blue states' power," Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., said in a statement in September announcing legislation that would call for reapportioning congressional seats before the 2028 election while excluding noncitizens and adding a citizenship question the 2030 census. The proposal has 42 Republican co-sponsors.Normally, seats are reapportioned every 10 years using new census data."Amid high stakes and slim margins, Congress must act before the 2028 elections to ensure only American citizens decide how congressional maps are drawn and who resides in the White House," Clyde added.Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., introduced similar legislation last year that would require the Census Bureau to include a citizenship status question on any future census, arguing noncitizens heavily skew the congressional map."While people continue to flee Democrat-run cities, desperate Democrats have back-filled the mass exodus with illegal immigrants so that they do not lose their seats in Congress or their electoral votes, hence artificially boosting their political power and in turn diluting the power of other Americans' votes," Hagerty said in a statement.Next U.S. census is in 2030The census changes are not final, but any change the administration implements would be difficult to undo before the 2030 census.The administration in its proposal states that "the Census Bureau is considering how best to distinguish between foreign citizens in the United States who are counted for apportionment" and suggests it would use administrative records to check the legal status of those counted. The proposal also says that the Census Bureau could add an immigration status question to the census' short-form questionnaire.The first, Anand said, would likely have the effect of suppressing response rates and contribute to an inaccurate count. The second would likely lead to errors and the wrongful discounting of people in the country with legal status.A New York Times analysis of the proposal found that it would result in lost House seats in several states, including places that generally favor Republicans. Florida, Rhode Island and Texas would all stand to lose a seat, according to the Times, while Minnesota, Ohio and Oregon could each add a representative to their congressional delegations.But beyond apportioning congressional seats, the rule could reduce funding for federal programs aimed at low-income populations, such as Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Head Start, said Julie Morita, president and CEO of the Joyce Foundation, a nonpartisan philanthropy that supports racial equity and economic mobility in the Great Lakes region. She noted these programs amount to "trillions of dollars.""An inaccurate count risks a decade of consequences," Rep. Grace Meng, D-N.Y., said in a statement in September. "Census data help determine representation in Congress, electoral districts, and the allocation of federal resources for health care, education, infrastructure, and other essential services." Trump has tried to exclude noncitizens beforeIn the waning days of his first term, Trump attempted to exclude undocumented immigrants from congressional apportionment, though the change wasn't implemented. In August 2025, Trump announced in a TruthSocial post that he'd instructed the Department of Commerce to "begin work on a new and highly accurate CENSUS.""People who are in our Country illegally WILL NOT BE COUNTED IN THE CENSUS," Trump posted.The Commerce Department has authority over the count, but must present to Congress any changes in subjects and the types of information to be compiled at least three years before the next Census Day, which would set an April 1, 2027, deadline. The department is also required to report to Congress the questions that will be included in the census at least two years before Census Day.Congress does have the authority to overrule proposed changes with legislation. But unless Democrats win a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, overruling the Trump administration is unlikely.A Democratic president who wins election in 2028 could also introduce a new rule to cancel out Trump's exclusion of certain immigrants, but the rule-making process is time-consuming and cumbersome, and there would be little time."Planning for the census takes lots of time, effort, research, operational changes, programming of computers, developing code," Anand said.

schema.headline: Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs critics toward legal fight

title: French supermarket fridges get hacked, heating to 122°F and sparking fires
description: A customer enters an Intermarche supermarket in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on October 12, 2026, , following a cyberattack affecti
body: A customer enters an Intermarche supermarket in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on October 12, 2026, , following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarche and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. Dimitar Dilkoff | Afp | Getty ImagesHackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires. Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday. Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores." "Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post. watch nowCNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article. "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday. "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality." AI enhancing cyberattacksLes Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC. It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores. TOPSHOT - A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on October 12, 2026, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost.Fred Tanneau | Afp | Getty Images"Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported."They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages. Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize, which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open. This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information.Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran.Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution."Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

schema.headline: French supermarket fridges get hacked, heating to 122°F and sparking fires

title: Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout
description: Tech stocks plummeted on Tuesday after a Chinese memory chipmaker said it had made significant progress in developing new and more efficient designs.
body: Tech stocks plummeted on Tuesday after a Chinese memory chipmaker said it had made significant progress in developing new and more efficient designs. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, announced over the weekend it had made headway on new architecture which will increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. The announcement spooked the market because CXMT is China's leading rival to global memory makers including Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung. And, until a recent blockbuster IPO, it was little known outside of its home market.Micron was down 3.7% in premarket trading, while SK Hynix's South Korean-listed shares closed 10% lower and Samsung Electronics fell 7.4%. Other memory-related stocks, including SanDisk, Seagate and Western Digital, were all lower.Blockbuster IPOCXMT leapt onto the global consciousness with its initial public offering in July.The company soared nearly 466% in its debut on Shanghai's tech-heavy STAR Market, making it the most valuable China-listed company at the time.Shares have since declined by 4% from their IPO-day price of 49 yuan per share, but the company maintains a market cap of 3.46 trillion Chinese yuan ($520 billion), not far off tech giant Tencent's 3.87 trillion yuan.watch nowHeadquartered in Hefei, CXMT's listing came roughly a decade on from its founding in 2016.One of the biggest questions for CXMT after its IPO was whether it would be able to narrow the capability gap with Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, particularly in high-bandwidth memory — a key component of AI chip systems. While huge domestic demand is supporting CXMT, it still faces challenges accessing chipmaking equipment, which has been effectively barred from China by U.S. export controls, including ASML's extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography machines, which are needed to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors.CXMT reportedly plans to roll out a new server-memory product based on new cell architecture by the end of 2026. The new design allows higher storage density, based on "4F square" tech. 4F square designs are also being pursued by SK Hynix, which in 2025 presented a roadmap for developing the tech. CXMT is often seen by analysts as trailing global competitors at the frontier of memory developments, and any news of breakthroughs can have a significant impact on investor perception of global rivals' market advantages.Market gainsCXMT has made significant market gains, despite challenges related to export controls. Its share of the global dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, market has risen to around 10%, up from about 4% a year ago, according to an HSBC note from Thursday."While US government is unlikely to allow made in China memory sales to US, sales to data centers in other regions like Europe could indirectly impact Micron," Citi analysts said in a note from August. Apple has started testing CXMT's DRAM chips for devices sold within China and was lobbying the U.S. government to permit broader use of the company's products, the Financial Times reported in July, citing people familiar with the matter. Apple has been approached for comment.

schema.headline: Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout

title: SpaceX agrees to testify to NYC Council about AI safety after receiving subpoena
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesSpaceX has agreed to testify before the New York City Council this week as part of a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, the council announced on Tuesday.The council said in a press release that the hearing will take place on Friday at 10 a.m. ET in front of its tech committee. Julie Menin, council speaker, and Nwamaka Ejebe, general counsel, issued a subpoena to Elon Musk and SpaceX's AI unit on Sept. 28, compelling testimony for a hearing that took place last week.Representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta all testified at the hearing on Oct. 5, but SpaceX did not appear. Menin said in Tuesday's statement that SpaceX agreed two days later to testify after the council said it intended to have its subpoena enforced by a judge."Last Monday, we held a major, hours-long hearing with whistleblowers, the world's largest tech companies, and the nation's foremost experts in AI," Menin said in Tuesday's release. "Conspicuously absent was SpaceXAI, which is unacceptable."Musk folded his AI venture, xAI, into SpaceX in February, creating a conglomerate that includes its Grok models, which are used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon. SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at over $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX also completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor.SpaceX competes with Anthropic and OpenAI in the AI market, though Grok trails far behind models from top rivals. The NYC council opened its investigation following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models.In its original letter ordering testimony from Musk or another SpaceX leader, the council said its investigation would help, "assess whether fast-emerging risks to public safety, cybersecurity, economic stability, privacy, consumers and businesses warrant immediate legislative action to protect New Yorkers."SpaceX's "failure to comply" with the subpoena, the council warned, could subject the company to penalties or other punishment under New York City laws and regulations. Carmen De La Rosa, chair of the tech committee, told CNBC in a statement that the council expects answers from SpaceX. "With the proliferation of Elon Musk's technology at the federal level, it is even more important they come to the discussion with robust context about data privacy, safeguards, and whistleblower protections," she said.Lawsuits are piling up against SpaceX after Grok's image generator enabled mass production and distribution of deepfake porn based on images of real people who did consent.SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed reporting.WATCH: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google execs testify at NYC Council meeting

schema.headline: SpaceX agrees to testify to NYC Council about AI safety after receiving subpoena
